title: Above the line on average
hook: Overall coverage is above the herd threshold. Can an outbreak still grow somewhere?

knows: R is the average number of people one case infects
doesNotKnow: that the threshold applies inside each group that mixes, not to a national average

misconception: If overall coverage is above the threshold, no outbreak can grow anywhere.
objective: The learner can explain that with R0 = 12, a town at 88% has R = 1.44 and can sustain spread even when the two-town average (93%) is above the 91.7% threshold, because the threshold applies within each mixing group.

claims.text: With R0 = 12 and perfect protection, the herd threshold is 1 - 1/12 = 91.7%.
claims.source: 1 - 1/R0 (Anderson & May 1991, Infectious Diseases of Humans, ch. 5).

claims.text: In a town with 88% vaccinated, R = 12 x 0.12 = 1.44, so an outbreak can grow there; at 98%, R = 12 x 0.02 = 0.24; two equal towns at 98% and 88% average 93%.
claims.source: Arithmetic; computed in Demo.tsx (rIn, comb), the same functions that label the stage.

claims.text: Raising coverage in a town whose people never meet another town raises the average but does not change R in the other town.
claims.source: Follows from the model's assumption of no contact between towns.

claims.text: The model is a made-up disease: no contact between the towns, random mixing inside each, perfect vaccine protection.
claims.source: Model choice in Demo.tsx; stated in the question, on the stage ('Toy: R0 12, no contact between towns') and in the reveal.

recall.question: A toy country has two separate regions of equal size, 99% and 85% vaccinated, for a disease with R0 = 10 (threshold 90%). Can an outbreak grow in the 85% region?
options: Only if the 99% region is hit too
recall.why: The threshold applies inside each mixing group: 10 x 0.15 = 1.5, above 1, whatever the average is.
